Mathematical analysis of an in-host model of viral dynamics with spatial heterogeneityThanks: The first author is supported by NSF grant DMS-1211667

Abstract.

We consider a spatially-heterogeneous generalization of a well-established model for the dynamics of the Human Immunodeficiency Virus-type 1 (HIV) within a susceptible host. The model consists of a nonlinear system of three coupled reaction-diffusion equations with parameters that may vary spatially. Upon formulating the model, we prove that it preserves the positivity of initial data and construct global-in-time solutions that are both bounded and smooth. Finally, additional results concerning the local and global asymptotic behavior of these solutions are also provided.

Key words and phrases: 
Global existence, HIV, Nonlinear diffusion, longtime asymptotic behavior
1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 35K51, 92C17, 35Q92; Secondary: 35K45, 35K57, 92C50, 35B40.

1. Introduction

Over the past few decades, considerable effort has been devoted to modeling the in-host dynamics of viral infection, and in particular, HIV infection within humans. These models have made significant contributions to the understanding of HIV pathogenesis in vivo and the mechanisms through which the infection may be mitigated. The typical response to viral infection within a host is the activation of the immune system, driving the level of virions down. If the immune response is sufficiently potent then the disease can be completely eradicated from the body, but often this does not occur. Instead, over a time period that can vary from weeks to months, an eventual balance of viral replication and clearance of the virus by the immune system occurs, leading to a state known as chronic infection. These equilibrium outcomes - viral clearance versus the development of a chronic infection - are suggestive of simple dynamics, but this ignores spatial variations including possible localized regions of infection, which alter the behavior in both transient and long time asymptotics [11].

Although some mathematical modeling of acute HIV infection has been performed [4, 18, 29], many current models focus on the time course of infection during the chronic stage, such as the response to antiretroviral therapy and HIV levels after the viral setpoint has been established [1, 27]. Moreover, because of the intricate complexity and the enormous number of cells involved, mathematical descriptions have generally been limited to nonlinear systems of a few coupled ordinary differential equations describing the average behavior throughout the whole body under the assumption that the environment is well-mixed or spatially-homogeneous [9, 25]. Unfortunately, such an assumption is not valid during the earliest stages of infection or at sites of viral entry, for instance, the vaginal or rectal epithelium during sexual transmission of HIV.

Indeed, viral propagation is a fundamentally local process. Focal bursts of virions have been demonstrated near infected T-cells in vivo [11, 17, 28]. Correlations between spatial location and viral genetics have been observed and modeled within splenic tissue [3, 7]. Localization is particularly relevant in the case of HIV infection, for a number of reasons. First, the virus is inherently unstable, possibly due to shedding of the glycoprotein gp120, which mediates the virus-cell binding process [15]. Spatially-heterogeneous outcomes may arise from underlying heterogeneity within tissue architecture, but it is also possible to observe such non-uniformities emerge spontaneously from the infection dynamics. Finally, an important aspect of the in-host spread of HIV is that the vast majority of infection occurs only in lymphoid tissues, where target cells are densely packed. This particular environment allows the virus to maximize the efficiency of diffusive transfer from infected producers to target cells. Thus, the local propagation of HIV within lymphoid tissue is fundamentally different in comparison to the hematogenous spread of the virus to other distant tissues [10, 31]. For all of these reasons, advances in modeling spatial aspects of the development and spread of viral infection within a host are crucial to furthering our understanding of viral pathogenesis and treatment.

Though this paper constitutes the first mathematical study of a model using a system of partial differential equations to study the spatial dependence of infection dynamics, others have used different mathematical mechanisms to model the incorporation of spatial fluctuations and correlations. Funk et al [8] posited a discrete lattice model to study the spatial dynamics of virions and T-cells, but provided only computational results and did not allow for motion or infection away from a fixed grid. Strain et al [31] studied the competition between viral lability and diffusion using a spatial cellular automaton model with a fixed T-cell background. Finally, Brauner et al [2] studied a system of coupled ODEs and a single PDE that allowed for the diffusion of virions within a two-dimensional medium under the assumption that T-cells remained motionless. However, their study did not focus on the well-posedness or global dynamical behavior of the model, or allow for cellular diffusion.

In order to investigate the impact of spatial dynamics in a simple mathematical model of HIV infection we extend the standard lumped or three-component model of in-host viral dynamics [1, 13, 19, 20, 26] to include spatially random diffusion and a spatially-dependent T-cell supply rate. Upon describing the model, we establish basic results concerning the well-posedness of smooth solutions and then focus mainly on their longtime asymptotic behavior. The overall goals are to establish a mathematical framework under which the spatial propagation of infection may be studied and to elucidate the contribution of the parameter space on the dynamical properties of solutions.

This paper proceeds as follows. In the next section, we introduce the spatial model of in-host viral dynamics and state our main results concerning existence, uniqueness, regularity, and longtime behavior of solutions to this system of semilinear PDEs. The proofs of these theorems are contained within Section 3, and finally proofs of associated lemmas are included within Section 4. Throughout the paper CC will denote a positive constant that may change from line to line. When necessary, we will denote the dependence of this constant on other parameters using subscripts, for instance Ct∗C_{t^{*}}.

2. Spatial Model of Viral Dynamics and Main Results

2.1. Derivation of the model

We begin with the standard, spatially-homogeneous model for in-host virus dynamics, given by

d​Td​t=λ−μT​T−k​T​V,d​Id​t=k​T​V−μI​I,d​Vd​t=N​μI​I−μV​V.}\left.\begin{aligned} \frac{dT}{dt}&=\lambda-\mu_{T}T-kTV,\\ \frac{dI}{dt}&=kTV-\mu_{I}I,\\ \frac{dV}{dt}&=N\mu_{I}I-\mu_{V}V.\end{aligned}\right\} (1)

Here, the unknown quantities are the populations of (i) uninfected target cells, denoted by T⁡(t)T(t) (in the study of HIV, these are CD4 T-cells); (ii) infected cells, denoted by I⁡(t)I(t); and (iii) free virions V⁡(t)V(t). It is assumed within the model that target cells are supplied at a constant rate λ\lambda and removed either through infection via contact with virions at a rate of kk per virion, or through natural cell death with per capita rate μT\mu_{T}. Similarly, μI\mu_{I} represents the per capita rate at which infected cells are destroyed, either through natural cell death, interaction with the body’s immune response, or via lysis due to new virions bursting from the cell membrane, while μV\mu_{V} represents the per capita rate at which virions are cleared from the body. Additionally, NN represents the “burst rate” of the virus, or the average number of new virions produced over the entire lifespan of an infected cell.

In order to introduce spatial variations within each population, we first let Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a given bounded domain with ∂Ω\partial\Omega smooth. As we desire a reformulation that preserves the general biological mechanisms of infection dynamics, we consider the system

∂tT−DT​Δ​T=λ⁡(x)−μT​T−k​T​V,∂tI−DI​Δ​I=k​T​V−μI​I,∂tV−DV​Δ​V=N​μI​I−μV​V}\left.\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}T-D_{T}\Delta T&=\lambda(x)-\mu_{T}T-kTV,\\ \partial_{t}I-D_{I}\Delta I&=kTV-\mu_{I}I,\\ \partial_{t}V-D_{V}\Delta V&=N\mu_{I}I-\mu_{V}V\end{aligned}\right\} (3CM)

for x∈Ωx\in\Omega, t≥0t\geq 0, which describes a spatially-heterogeneous three-component model in which all populations may diffuse throughout a fixed region of the body and the supply rate of new susceptible cells is spatially-dependent, rather than constant. Hence, TT, II, and VV now represent concentrations of healthy cells, infected cells, and virions, respectively. The diffusive nature of cell transport is, by now, well-known both in-vivo and in-vitro, and while there may be some minor evidence for this motion to occur via fractional or anomalous diffusion [12], we assume a standard diffusive mechanism via Brownian motion as suggested by [16]. As spatial effects are present, the domain Ω\Omega might be considered as an entry point of viral infection, such as the vaginal or rectal epithelium during sexual contact. Additionally, one does not expect the introduction of new T-cells to occur uniformly throughout the domain, and thus, we allow for spatial variations in the function λ⁡(x)\lambda(x) rather than taking this parameter to be constant as in (1).

With the spatial domain fixed, the coupled, nonlinear system of PDEs is augmented by the initial conditions

T⁡(0,x)=T0​(x),I⁡(0,x)=I0​(x),V⁡(0,x)=V0​(x).T(0,x)=T_{0}(x),\quad I(0,x)=I_{0}(x),\quad V(0,x)=V_{0}(x).

Throughout, we make some standard biological assumptions on the initial concentrations, namely

T0​(x),I0​(x),V0​(x)​are continuous, positive, and bounded functions on​Ω¯T_{0}(x),I_{0}(x),V_{0}(x)\ \mbox{are continuous, positive, and bounded functions on}\ \bar{\Omega} (A1)

Additionally, we consider the separate cases of homogeneous Dirichlet or Neumann boundary conditions, so that (3CM) is supplemented by either of the two conditions

w(t,x)=0on[0,∞)×∂Ωw(t,x)=0\quad\mathrm{on}\ [0,\infty)\times\partial\Omega (BC1)
∂w∂n(t,x)=0on[0,∞)×∂Ω\frac{\partial w}{\partial n}(t,x)=0\quad\mathrm{on}\ [0,\infty)\times\partial\Omega (BC2)

for ww replaced by T,IT,I, and VV, respectively.

The biological parameters k,N,μT,μI,μVk,N,\mu_{T},\mu_{I},\mu_{V} and diffusion coefficients DT,DI,DVD_{T},D_{I},D_{V} are all positive constants. For simplicity, we assume throughout that λ∈C∞​(Ω)\lambda\in C^{\infty}\left(\Omega\right) with λ⁡(x)≥0\lambda(x)\geq 0 for x∈Ωx\in\Omega and λ≢0\lambda\not\equiv 0.

With this framework in place, we make a few remarks concerning the generality of the model. First, this model can be used to study a wide-range of viral infections, including HIV, Hepatitis B (HBV), Hepatitis C (HCV), Human T-cell Leukemia Virus (HTLV), and Human Cytomegalo Virus (CMV) [1, 20], but we mainly focus on the case of HIV as in-host modeling has significantly furthered the understanding of this particular disease in recent years. Additionally, though we will deal with the case of Ω\Omega bounded, it is straightforward to use our techniques to establish analogous well-posedness results for the problem posed on the whole space (i.e., Ω=ℝn\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{n}). In fact, this problem is easier to approach as one has an exact representation of the associated heat kernel

Φ⁡(t,x)=1(4​π​t)n/2​exp⁡{−|x|24​t},x∈Ω,t>0\Phi(t,x)=\frac{1}{(4\pi t)^{n/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{\left|x\right|^{2}}{4t}\right\},\,\,\,x\in\Omega,\,\,t>0

and this is the only significant alteration within the associated proofs. In the case of Ω=ℝn\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{n}, one would need to assume T0,I0T_{0},I_{0}, and V0V_{0} decay suitably fast as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty, for instance

T0​(x)≤C​|x|−αT_{0}(x)\leq C|x|^{-\alpha}

for some α>n\alpha>n, C>0C>0, and any x∈Ωx\in\Omega, in lieu of boundary conditions. Of course, for this particular application a bounded domain is certainly more natural, and we will typically have in mind the case of Neumann boundary conditions. Additionally, the cases of n=1,2,3n=1,2,3 are the most reasonable choices, but our results will actually be independent of dimension. Hence, we are able to derive sharp conditions on parameters that guarantee the local and global asymptotic stability of solutions regardless of the inherent spatial dimension. Additionally, though it is assumed throughout that λ⁡(x)\lambda(x) is smooth, one may relax this assumption and arrive at similar conclusions regarding global-in-time solutions and their dynamical properties. Finally, another reasonable assumption to include within the model would be to take DI=DTD_{I}=D_{T}, as infection of susceptible cells should not influence the rate of diffusion. However, such a condition will not be needed within the analysis, and hence we omit it. With the model well formulated, we state the main results of the paper.

2.2. Existence of Solutions, Positivity, and a priori Bounds

Our first result is quite standard and serves to merely establish the existence of a suitable solution for small time.

Theorem 2.1 (Local Existence).

Assume condition (A1) holds, then there is t∗∈[0,∞]t^{*}\in[0,\infty] such that (3CM) with (BC1)/(BC2) has a unique, positive solution (T,I,V)∈C1​((0,t∗),C2​(Ω))×C1​((0,t∗),C2​(Ω))×C1​((0,t∗),C2​(Ω))(T,I,V)\in C^{1}((0,t^{*});C^{2}(\Omega))\times C^{1}\left((0,t^{*});C^{2}(\Omega)\right)\times C^{1}\left((0,t^{*});C^{2}(\Omega)\right).

We will omit the proof as the techniques are well-known in classical literature, and the result can be obtained by a straightforward application of the Contraction Mapping Principle. With a local-in-time solution in hand, we turn our attention to its properties, including positivity (assuming positive initial data), boundedness, and its extension globally in time.

Theorem 2.2 (Positivity, Bounds, and Global Existence).

Assume the initial data satisfy (A1). Then, for any t∗>0t^{*}>0, there exist T,I,VT,I,V satisfying (3CM) on (0,t∗)×Ω(0,t^{*})\times\Omega, the initial conditions, and boundary condition (BC1)/(BC2). Furthermore, we have T⁡(t,x),I⁡(t,x),V⁡(t,x)>0T(t,x),I(t,x),V(t,x)>0 for all x∈Ω,t∈[0,t∗]x\in\Omega,t\in[0,t^{*}], and there are C,Ct∗>0C,C_{t^{*}}>0 such that the solutions satisfy

||T⁡(t)||∞≤C\left|\left|T(t)\right|\right|_{\infty}\leq C

and

||I⁡(t)||∞+||V⁡(t)||∞≤Ct∗\left|\left|I(t)\right|\right|_{\infty}+\left|\left|V(t)\right|\right|_{\infty}\leq C_{t^{*}}

for all t∈[0,t∗].t\in[0,t^{*}].

A few comments regarding the global existence of solutions are in order. Specifically, it should be noted that the idea of “mass transfer” among concentrations is a crucial aspect of this model. Consider, for instance, what would occur if the sign of the k​T​VkTV term in the first equation were changed, so that TT satisfied the evolution equation

(∂t−DTΔ)T=λ(x)−μTT+kTV.(\partial_{t}-D_{T}\Delta)T=\lambda(x)-\mu_{T}T+kTV.

Then, even in the simpler case of λ≡0\lambda\equiv 0, it can be shown that this model mimics the behavior of the related nonlinear system

(∂tu−Δ​u)=u​v,(∂tv−Δ​v)=u​v(\partial_{t}u-\Delta u)=uv,\qquad(\partial_{t}v-\Delta v)=uv

under a suitable transformation of the unknown quantities. Using tools similar to those established in [5, 32], it can be shown that solutions to this system blow-up in finite time. Hence, the exact transfer, rather than addition of the nonlinear terms is crucial to the existence theory, as is the continued positivity of solutions. In addition, Theorem 2.2 demonstrates further that the effect of a continuing supply of T-cells, given by λ⁡(x)≥0\lambda(x)\geq 0, does not lead to a blow-up in the system

Now that we have established that solutions exist globally in time, we note that generally, the diffusion operator (∂t−DΔ)(\partial_{t}-D\Delta) has a smoothing effect on initial data, so we expect some gain in regularity in the concentrations. More specifically, assuming that the initial data is in L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega), we expect that solutions not only remain in L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega) but actually possess weak derivatives in this space as well.

Theorem 2.3 (Regularity).

Let t∗>0t^{*}>0 be given. If T,I,VT,I,V satisfy (3CM) on (0,t∗)×Ω(0,t^{*})\times\Omega and T0,I0,V0∈L2​(Ω)T_{0},I_{0},V_{0}\in L^{2}\left(\Omega\right) with (BC1)/(BC2), then ∇T​(t,⋅),∇I​(t,⋅),∇V​(t,⋅)∈L2​(Ω)\nabla T(t,\cdot),\nabla I(t,\cdot),\nabla V(t,\cdot)\in L^{2}\left(\Omega\right) for all t∈(0,t∗)t\in(0,t^{*}). In fact, T⁡(t,⋅),I⁡(t,⋅),V⁡(t,⋅)∈Hm​(Ω)T(t,\cdot),I(t,\cdot),V(t,\cdot)\in H^{m}\left(\Omega\right) for all t∈(0,t∗)t\in(0,t^{*}) and m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}.

2.3. Asymptotic Behavior of Solutions

Finally, with the well-posedness of solutions understood, we turn our attention to their longtime asymptotic behavior. In particular, we study both the local and global stability properties of the uninfected steady state, described below. Of course, any time-independent solution, i.e. a triple (T⁡(x),I⁡(x),V⁡(x))(T(x),I(x),V(x)), must satisfy the nonlinear elliptic system

−DT​Δ​T=λ⁡(x)−μT​T−k​T​V−DI​Δ​I=k​T​V−μI​I−DV​Δ​V=N​μI​I−μV​V}\left.\begin{aligned} -D_{T}\Delta T&=\lambda(x)-\mu_{T}T-kTV\\ -D_{I}\Delta I&=kTV-\mu_{I}I\\ -D_{V}\Delta V&=N\mu_{I}I-\mu_{V}V\end{aligned}\right\} (2)

which may have many solutions for differing parameter values. In particular, we focus on the unique uninfected state Ec:=(T∞​(x),0,0)E_{c}:=(T_{\infty}(x),0,0), which represents the ultimate clearance of the virus, where T∞T_{\infty} satisfies the linear boundary value problem

−DT​Δ​T∞=λ⁡(x)−μT​T∞-D_{T}\Delta T_{\infty}=\lambda(x)-\mu_{T}T_{\infty} (3)

for x∈Ωx\in\Omega with boundary conditions given by (BC1)/(BC2). We first summarize some useful properties of the steady-state T-cell count.

Theorem 2.4.

The function T∞T_{\infty} defined by (3) with (BC1)/(BC2) is C∞C^{\infty} and satisfies

0≤T∞​(x)≤‖λ‖∞μT0\leq T_{\infty}(x)\leq\frac{\|\lambda\|_{\infty}}{\mu_{T}}

for every x∈Ωx\in\Omega with T∞≢0T_{\infty}\not\equiv 0.

In order to determine the stability of the aforementioned equilibrium state, we are first led to study the system (2) linearized about EcE_{c}, namely

−DT​Δ​T=λ⁡(x)−μT​T−k​T∞​(x)​V−DI​Δ​I=k​T∞​(x)​V−μI​I−DV​Δ​V=N​μI​I−μV​V}\left.\begin{aligned} -D_{T}\Delta T&=\lambda(x)-\mu_{T}T-kT_{\infty}(x)V\\ -D_{I}\Delta I&=kT_{\infty}(x)V-\mu_{I}I\\ -D_{V}\Delta V&=N\mu_{I}I-\mu_{V}V\end{aligned}\right\} (4)

with boundary conditions (BC1)/(BC2). Here, the first equation decouples from the last two and we need only study the PDEs describing I⁡(x)I(x) and V⁡(x)V(x). Accordingly, we define the second-order, linear self-adjoint operator

ℒ=∇⋅(D∇)+M(x)\mathcal{L}=\nabla\cdot(D\nabla)+M(x) (5)

on the Hilbert space

ℋ={ϕ∈H2​(Ω)×H2​(Ω):ϕ1​and​ϕ2​satisfy​(BC1)/(BC2)}\mathcal{H}=\left\{\phi\in H^{2}(\Omega)\times H^{2}(\Omega):\phi_{1}\ \mathrm{and}\ \phi_{2}\ \mathrm{satisfy}\ \eqref{BC1}/\eqref{BC2}\right\}

where

D=diag⁡(DI,DV)andM⁡(x)=[−μIk​T∞​(x)N​μI−μV].D=\mathrm{diag}(D_{I},D_{V})\qquad\mathrm{and}\qquad M(x)=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}-\mu_{I}&kT_{\infty}(x)\\ N\mu_{I}&-\mu_{V}\end{array}\right]. (6)

We note that ℒ\mathcal{L} is a negative operator if −M⁡(x)-M(x) is a positive semi-definite matrix. Because μI>0\mu_{I}>0 this latter condition is implied by det(−M⁡(x))>0\det(-M(x))>0 for all x∈Ωx\in\Omega. After some algebra, this condition is exactly ‖R0‖∞<1\|R_{0}\|_{\infty}<1 where

R0​(x):=N​k​T∞​(x)μV.R_{0}(x):=\frac{NkT_{\infty}(x)}{\mu_{V}}. (7)

The stability properties of EcE_{c} then depend crucially on the greatest real part of the spectrum of ℒ\mathcal{L}, namely

η0:=sup{Re⁡(η):η∈σ⁡(A)}.\eta_{0}:=\sup\{\mathrm{Re}(\eta):\eta\in\sigma(A)\}. (8)

Due to the compactness of the inverse of ℒ\mathcal{L}, it is well-known that σ⁡(ℒ)\sigma(\mathcal{L}) consists only of eigenvalues and, when ordered, these form a decreasing sequence of real numbers diverging to −∞-\infty. Additionally, η0\eta_{0} can be uniquely identified using the associated Rayleigh quotient

η0=supψ∈ℋψ≠0{∫Ωψ⁡(x)⋅ℒ​ψ​(x)​𝑑x∫Ω|ψ⁡(x)|2​𝑑x}.\eta_{0}=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\psi\in\mathcal{H}\\ \psi\neq 0\end{subarray}}\left\{\frac{\int_{\Omega}\psi(x)\cdot\mathcal{L}\psi(x)\ dx}{\int_{\Omega}|\psi(x)|^{2}\ dx}\right\}.

Hence, the sign of the parameter η0\eta_{0} will determine whether all eigenvalues are negative, ensuring that solutions which begin sufficiently close tend to the equilibrium state, or whether a positive eigenvalue exists, thereby creating instabilities within the system. Prior to stating the stability and instability results for the viral clearance state, we first show that under particular conditions it is the unique biologically-feasible solution of the steady state system (2).

Theorem 2.5.

If η0<0\eta_{0}<0 then the triple (T∞​(x),0,0)(T_{\infty}(x),0,0) is the unique nonnegative solution of (2) with (BC1)/(BC2).

Next, we characterize the local stability properties of the clearance state. In the spatially-homogeneous case, as in many other biological systems, it is known that a single parameter dictates the dynamical structure of solutions. With regards to (1), the quantity known as the basic reproductive ratio, defined by R0:=λ​k​NμT​μVR_{0}:=\frac{\lambda kN}{\mu_{T}\mu_{V}}, describes the entire long time behavior of the infection. In this case the spatially-independent T-cell count is T∞=λμTT_{\infty}=\frac{\lambda}{\mu_{T}}, which means that R0​(x)R_{0}(x) as defined by (7) is exactly the basic reproductive ratio. Additionally, the associated principal eigenvalue is η0=R0−1\eta_{0}=R_{0}-1. Though R0R_{0} for the spatially-heterogeneous system is now a function rather than a single value, we may still characterize the dynamics in terms of the single parameter η0\eta_{0}. Hence, the following local stability theorem establishes a parameter regime that generalizes the spatially-homogeneous model, in which the longtime asymptotics are still shown to be determined only by the sign of η0\eta_{0}.

Theorem 2.6.

Let T,I,VT,I,V satisfy (3CM) with (BC1)/(BC2). If η0<0\eta_{0}<0 then the viral clearance state EcE_{c} is locally asymptotically stable. If η0>0\eta_{0}>0, then it is unstable.

Finally, we study the global dynamics of this steady state. Our first global result shows that the T-cell population tends to T∞​(x)T_{\infty}(x) exponentially fast for any initial data and within any parameter regime.

Theorem 2.7.

Let T,I,VT,I,V satisfy (3CM) with (BC1)/(BC2). Then, for every t≥0t\geq 0

‖T⁡(t)−T∞‖∞≤‖T0−T∞‖∞​e−μT​t.\|T(t)-T_{\infty}\|_{\infty}\leq\|T_{0}-T_{\infty}\|_{\infty}e^{-\mu_{T}t}.

In view of Theorems 2.5 and 2.6, we see that for η0<0\eta_{0}<0, EcE_{c} is locally stable and the only nonnegative equilibrium. Hence, one might expect that it is also globally stable in this case. While we do not have a proof of this result assuming only the condition η0<0\eta_{0}<0, we can do so under a slightly more restrictive assumption.

Theorem 2.8.

Let T,I,VT,I,V satisfy (3CM) with (BC1)/(BC2). If ‖R0‖∞<1\|R_{0}\|_{\infty}<1 then there are C0,a>0C_{0},a>0 such that

‖I⁡(t)‖∞+‖V⁡(t)‖∞≤C0​e−a​t\|I(t)\|_{\infty}+\|V(t)\|_{\infty}\leq C_{0}e^{-at}

for every t≥0t\geq 0.

Combining this result with Theorem 2.7 yields a sufficient condition under which the viral clearance state is a globally asymptotically stable equilibrium point of the system with exponential decay. Though it is beneficial to characterize the dynamics of solutions, it may be difficult to explicitly determine T∞T_{\infty} for given parameter values and domain Ω\Omega. Hence, our final result provides an additional sufficient condition that can be readily computed to describe the global asymptotics of solutions.

Corollary 2.9.

Let T,I,VT,I,V satisfy (3CM) with (BC1)/(BC2). If N​k​‖λ‖∞μT​μV<1,\frac{Nk\|\lambda\|_{\infty}}{\mu_{T}\mu_{V}}<1, then the conclusion of Theorem 2.8 remains valid.

We note that the longtime behavior results are independent of both the diffusion coefficients DT,DI,DV>0D_{T},D_{I},D_{V}>0 and the dimension n=1,2,3n=1,2,3. In the next section we prove the main results of the paper.

3. Proofs of Main Results

As previously mentioned, the proof of the first theorem is a fairly standard application of the Contraction Mapping Principle, and hence we omit it. Prior to proving Theorem 2.2, we establish a few minor lemmas regarding the scalar diffusion equation that arise from the Maximum Principle.

Lemma 3.1.

Let D>0D>0 and u0​(x)>0u_{0}(x)>0 for all x∈Ωx\in\Omega be given and assume that uu satisfies

(∂t−DΔ)u=g(t,x),x∈Ω,t>0u⁡(0,x)=u0​(x).x∈Ω}\left.\begin{array}[]{lr}&(\partial_{t}-D\Delta)u=g(t,x),\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,x\in\Omega,t>0\\ &u(0,x)=u_{0}(x).\hskip 39.83368ptx\in\Omega\end{array}\right\} (9)

If g⁡(t,x)≥0g(t,x)\geq 0 for all x∈Ω,t≥0x\in\Omega,t\geq 0, then u⁡(t,x)≥0u(t,x)\geq 0 for all x∈Ω,t≥0x\in\Omega,t\geq 0.
Additionally, if g⁡(t,x)>0g(t,x)>0 for all x∈Ω,t≥0x\in\Omega,t\geq 0, then u⁡(t,x)>0u(t,x)>0 for all x∈Ω,t≥0x\in\Omega,t\geq 0. That is, (∂t−DΔ)(\partial_{t}-D\Delta) preserves positivity on [0,∞)×Ω[0,\infty)\times\Omega.

The following corollaries, which will be useful throughout the remainder of this section, are then immediate consequences of this result.

Corollary 3.2.

If u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) satisfies (9) with D>0D>0, then

u(x,0)=u0(x),x∈Ω.\displaystyle u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\hskip 39.83368ptx\in\Omega.

Then u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) satisfies the same inequality as in Corollary 3.2. That is,

||u⁡(t)||∞≤||u0||∞+∫0t||g⁡(τ)||∞​𝑑τ, for all ​t∈[0,∞).\left|\left|u(t)\right|\right|_{\infty}\leq\left|\left|u_{0}\right|\right|_{\infty}+\int^{t}_{0}\left|\left|g(\tau)\right|\right|_{\infty}d\tau,\,\,\,\text{ for all }t\in[0,\infty).

With these results in place, we may now prove the global existence and positivity theorem.

Proof (Theorem 2.2).

Since the initial data is positive and solutions are smooth (see Theorem 2.3), the functions T⁡(t,x),I⁡(t,x),V⁡(t,x)T(t,x),I(t,x),V(t,x) must remain positive for all x∈Ωx\in\Omega and up to some time within the interval of existence [0,t∗).[0,t^{*}). Define the maximal time of positivity within this interval by

Q=sup{t∈[0,t∗)|T(s,x),I(s,x),V(s,x)>0 for all x∈Ω,s∈[0,t]}.Q=\sup\left\{t\in[0,t^{*})\,\,\biggr|\,\,T(s,x),I(s,x),V(s,x)>0\text{ for all }x\in\Omega,s\in[0,t]\right\}.

Estimating on this interval we find

(∂t−DTΔ)T+μTT≤λ(x).(\partial_{t}-D_{T}\Delta)T+\mu_{T}T\leq\lambda(x).

Multiplying by an integrating factor yields

(∂t−DTΔ)[eμT​tT]≤λ(x)eμT​t.(\partial_{t}-D_{T}\Delta)[e^{\mu_{T}t}T]\leq\lambda(x)e^{\mu_{T}t}.

By Corollary 3.3, we find

and upon integrating

||T⁡(t)||∞≤||T0||∞​e−μT​t+||λ||∞μT​(1−e−μT​t).\left|\left|T(t)\right|\right|_{\infty}\leq\left|\left|T_{0}\right|\right|_{\infty}e^{-\mu_{T}t}+\frac{\left|\left|\lambda\right|\right|_{\infty}}{\mu_{T}}\left(1-e^{-\mu_{T}t}\right).

In particular, we have a uniform bound for ||T⁡(t)||∞\left|\left|T(t)\right|\right|_{\infty} on [0,Q][0,Q], denoted by

TM:=||T0||∞+||λ||∞μT.T_{M}:=\left|\left|T_{0}\right|\right|_{\infty}+\frac{\left|\left|\lambda\right|\right|_{\infty}}{\mu_{T}}.

Next, we use the positivity of solutions and this uniform bound within the equations for II and VV. On the interval [0,Q][0,Q], we have (∂t−DIΔ)I≤kT(t,x)V(t,x)\left(\partial_{t}-D_{I}\Delta\right)I\leq kT(t,x)V(t,x). Using Corollary 3.3, this implies

||I⁡(t)||∞\displaystyle\left|\left|I(t)\right|\right|_{\infty} ≤||I0||∞+k​∫0t||T⁡(τ)​V​(τ)||∞​𝑑τ\displaystyle\leq\left|\left|I_{0}\right|\right|_{\infty}+k\int^{t}_{0}\left|\left|T(\tau)V(\tau)\right|\right|_{\infty}d\tau (10)
≤||I0||∞+k​TM​∫0t||V⁡(τ)||∞​𝑑τ\displaystyle\leq\left|\left|I_{0}\right|\right|_{\infty}+kT_{M}\int^{t}_{0}\left|\left|V(\tau)\right|\right|_{\infty}d\tau
≤C⁡(1+∫0t||V⁡(τ)||∞​dτ).\displaystyle\leq C\left(1+\int^{t}_{0}\left|\left|V(\tau)\right|\right|_{\infty}d\tau\right).

Using the positivity of II within the equation for VV, we have

(∂t−DVΔ)V≤NμII(t,x)(\partial_{t}-D_{V}\Delta)V\leq N\mu_{I}I(t,x)

for t∈[0,Q].t\in[0,Q]. Invoking Corollary 3.3 yields

||V⁡(t)||∞\displaystyle\left|\left|V(t)\right|\right|_{\infty} ≤||V0||∞+N​μI​∫0t||I⁡(τ)||∞​𝑑τ\displaystyle\leq\left|\left|V_{0}\right|\right|_{\infty}+N\mu_{I}\int^{t}_{0}\left|\left|I(\tau)\right|\right|_{\infty}d\tau (11)
≤C⁡(1+∫0t||I⁡(τ)||∞​dτ).\displaystyle\leq C\left(1+\int^{t}_{0}\left|\left|I(\tau)\right|\right|_{\infty}d\tau\right).

ϕ⁡(t)=||I⁡(t)||∞+||V⁡(t)||∞,t∈[0,Q].\phi(t)=\left|\left|I(t)\right|\right|_{\infty}+\left|\left|V(t)\right|\right|_{\infty},\,\,\,\,t\in[0,Q].

ϕ⁡(t)≤C⁡(1+∫0tϕ⁡(τ)​𝑑τ),t∈[0,Q].\phi(t)\leq C\left(1+\int^{t}_{0}\phi(\tau)d\tau\right),\,\,\,\,t\in[0,Q].

Finally, for the TT equation, we use the local-in-time bound on ||V⁡(t)||∞\left|\left|V(t)\right|\right|_{\infty} to find

(∂t−DTΔ)T\displaystyle(\partial_{t}-D_{T}\Delta)T ≥λ−μT​T−k​T​(t,x)​||V⁡(t)||∞\displaystyle\geq\lambda-\mu_{T}T-kT(t,x)\left|\left|V(t)\right|\right|_{\infty}
≥λ−μT​T−C​eC​t​T\displaystyle\geq\lambda-\mu_{T}T-Ce^{Ct}T

and ζ⁡(0)​T​(0,x)=T0​(x)\zeta(0)T(0,x)=T_{0}(x). Thus, by Lemma 3.1, we have ζ⁡(t)​T​(x,t)>0\zeta(t)T(x,t)>0, and hence T⁡(t,x)>0T(t,x)>0 for t∈[0,Q]t\in[0,Q]. Therefore, solutions remain strictly positive throughout the interval [0,Q][0,Q] and this implies Q=t∗Q=t^{*}, the maximal time of existence. Of course, since the solution remains bounded on this interval as well, we find t∗=∞t^{*}=\infty and the proof is complete. ∎

Next, we turn to the proofs of the regularity results. For brevity, we will prove the first statement only. However, the same technique can be applied to derive estimates inductively and prove the latter result without the introduction of new ideas. For additional background on the specifics of obtaining the second statement, we direct the reader to [22, 23] as the higher-order regularity stated here can be deduced by straightforwardly adapting the arguments in those previous works.

With the regularity proof complete, we finally study the longtime dynamical behavior of (3CM), and in particular, the viral clearance steady state EcE_{c}. We first prove some useful properties of T∞​(x)T_{\infty}(x).

Proof (Theorem 2.4).

To prove the nonnegativity of T∞T_{\infty}, we merely note that the Green’s function associated to the operator (−DT​Δ+μT)(-D_{T}\Delta+\mu_{T}) is positive [14], and hence the conclusion follows due to the nonnegativity of λ⁡(x)\lambda(x) on Ω\Omega. Additionally, T∞T_{\infty} inherits the regularity of λ\lambda and T∞≢0T_{\infty}\not\equiv 0 because G,λ≢0G,\lambda\not\equiv 0.

To prove the upper bound, we let G⁡(x)G(x) satisfy

If GG satisfies (BC2), we merely enforce the boundary conditions to conclude

If GG satisfies (BC1), we note that G=0G=0 on ∂Ω\partial\Omega and G⁡(x)>0G(x)>0 for x∈Ωx\in\Omega, therefore ∂G∂n≤0\frac{\partial G}{\partial n}\leq 0 on ∂Ω\partial\Omega and thus

∫ΩG⁡(x)​𝑑x≤1μT.\int_{\Omega}G(x)\ dx\leq\frac{1}{\mu_{T}}.

Again, since GG is positive, this further shows ‖G‖1≤1μT\|G\|_{1}\leq\frac{1}{\mu_{T}} in either case. Finally, since T∞T_{\infty} satisfies the inhomogeneous equation it must be given by T∞=G∗λT_{\infty}=G\ast\lambda and a simple convolution estimate yields

‖T∞‖∞=‖G∗λ‖∞≤‖λ‖∞​‖G‖1=‖λ‖∞μT.\|T_{\infty}\|_{\infty}=\|G\ast\lambda\|_{\infty}\leq\|\lambda\|_{\infty}\|G\|_{1}=\frac{\|\lambda\|_{\infty}}{\mu_{T}}.

∎

Next, we prove the uniqueness of this steady state when η0<0\eta_{0}<0.

can be rewritten as

Next, we prove the local stability and instability results. Since a generalization of the celebrated next generation method adapted to spatially-heterogeneous problems was recently developed in [33], we will rely on many of the results therein for the proof.

Proof (Theorem 2.6).

To prove the first conclusion, we assume η0<0\eta_{0}<0 and put the system (4) into the form of [33, Equation (3.9)]. The uninfected compartment - T⁡(t,x)T(t,x) - and infected compartments - I⁡(t,x)I(t,x) and V⁡(t,x)V(t,x) - can be separated into the scalar function uSu_{S} and vector function uIu_{I}, respectively. The equation for the latter can be represented as

∂tuI=∇⋅(D∇uI)+F(x)uI−V(x)uI\partial_{t}u_{I}=\nabla\cdot(D\nabla u_{I})+F(x)u_{I}-V(x)u_{I} (19)

where

uI​(t,x)=[I⁡(t,x)V⁡(t,x)],D=diag⁡(DI,DV),u_{I}(t,x)=\left[\begin{array}[]{c}I(t,x)\\ V(t,x)\end{array}\right],\quad D=\mathrm{diag}(D_{I},D_{V}),

and

F⁡(x)=[0k​T∞​(x)00],V⁡(x)=[μI0−N​μIμV].F(x)=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}0&kT_{\infty}(x)\\ 0&0\end{array}\right],\quad V(x)=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\mu_{I}&0\\ -N\mu_{I}&\mu_{V}\end{array}\right].

Using the properties of T∞T_{\infty} guaranteed by Theorem 2.4, we note that the system in this form satisfies assumptions (A11)-(A66) of [33]. Then, [33, Theorem 3.1] directly implies the conclusion under the assumption η0<0\eta_{0}<0, since this eigenvalue is exactly the spectral bound for the operator on the right side of (19). Therefore, EcE_{c} is a locally asymptotically stable equilibrium for (3CM).

To prove the second conclusion, we will show that the eigenvalue problem

∇⋅(D∇ϕ)+M(x)ϕ=ηϕ\nabla\cdot(D\nabla\phi)+M(x)\phi=\eta\phi (20)

with DD and MM defined by (6) possesses a positive eigenvalue with corresponding positive eigenvector under the assumption η0>0\eta_{0}>0. To this end, we will again utilize a result from [33]. From (6), we see that M⁡(x)M(x) is cooperative for all x∈Ωx\in\Omega and M⁡(x0)M(x_{0}) is irreducible for some x0∈Ωx_{0}\in\Omega since, by Theorem 2.4, T∞​(x)≥0T_{\infty}(x)\geq 0 for every x∈Ωx\in\Omega and T∞≢0T_{\infty}\not\equiv 0. Hence, by [33, Theorem 2.2], η0\eta_{0} as defined by (8) is an algebraically simple eigenvalue of (20) with a strongly positive eigenvector satisfying

Re(η)<η0forallη∈σ(∇⋅(D∇)+M)∖{η0}.\mathrm{Re}(\eta)<\eta_{0}\qquad\ \mathrm{for\ all}\ \eta\in\sigma\biggl(\nabla\cdot(D\nabla)+M\biggr)\setminus\{\eta_{0}\}.

Therefore, η0\eta_{0} is a positive eigenvalue with positive eigenfunction, and the instability of EcE_{c} follows immediately. Finally, we note that that these results are valid for either boundary condition (BC1) or (BC2) as mentioned in [33, Remarks 2.2 and 3.1]. ∎

With the local stability proof complete, we turn to the proofs of the global asymptotic behavior of the system.

Thus, the exponential decay of ‖V⁡(t)‖∞\|V(t)\|_{\infty} continues on this time interval and we merely require the constant within this inequality to be strictly dominated by C1​‖V⁡(0)‖∞C_{1}\|V(0)\|_{\infty} to complete the argument. After a brief calculation, we see that (24) implies

‖V⁡(0)‖∞+α2α2−a​C2≤M~​C1​‖V⁡(0)‖∞,\|V(0)\|_{\infty}+\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\alpha_{2}-a}C_{2}\leq\tilde{M}C_{1}\|V(0)\|_{\infty},

and combining this with the estimate above, we find

‖V⁡(t)‖∞≤M~​C1​‖V⁡(0)‖∞​e−a​t\|V(t)\|_{\infty}\leq\tilde{M}C_{1}\|V(0)\|_{\infty}e^{-at}

for any t∈[τ0,τ1]t\in[\tau_{0},\tau_{1}]. Since M~<1\tilde{M}<1, we see that τ1\tau_{1} cannot be finite, as this would contradict its definition as the supremum, and thus τ1=∞\tau_{1}=\infty. Therefore, using (25) the estimate

‖V⁡(t)‖∞≤C1​‖V⁡(0)‖∞​e−a​t\|V(t)\|_{\infty}\leq C_{1}\|V(0)\|_{\infty}e^{-at}

holds for all t≥0t\geq 0. Since we have ‖I⁡(t)‖∞≤C2​e−a​t\|I(t)\|_{\infty}\leq C_{2}e^{-at} on the same interval, the exponential decay of ‖I⁡(t)‖∞\|I(t)\|_{\infty} follows with the same rate. Taking C0=max⁡{C1,C2}C_{0}=\max\{C_{1},C_{2}\} yields a uniform decay estimate on both non-dimensionalized quantities, namely

||I⁡(t)||∞+||V⁡(t)||∞≤C0​e−a​t.\left|\left|I(t)\right|\right|_{\infty}+\left|\left|V(t)\right|\right|_{\infty}\leq C_{0}e^{-at}.

Finally, upon rescaling the non-dimensionalized system, the result holds for the original concentrations II and VV with a change in the constants C0C_{0} and aa.

∎

We end this section with the proof of the associated corollary.

Proof (Corollary 2.9).

Assuming the condition on the parameters holds, we note that ‖T∞‖∞≤‖λ‖∞μT\|T_{\infty}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\|\lambda\|_{\infty}}{\mu_{T}} by Theorem 2.4. Hence, N​k​‖λ‖∞μT​μV<1\frac{Nk\|\lambda\|_{\infty}}{\mu_{T}\mu_{V}}<1 implies

‖R0‖∞=N​k​‖T∞‖∞μV<1,\|R_{0}\|_{\infty}=\frac{Nk\|T_{\infty}\|_{\infty}}{\mu_{V}}<1,

and the assumptions of Theorem 2.8 are satisfied, which implies the result. ∎

4. Proofs of Lemmas

Finally, to complete the paper, we include the proofs of lemmas from the previous sections. The first few results are fairly straightforward applications of the ideas inherent within the Maximum Principle, but we include them for completeness.
